title: Nutrition
text: Nutrition information covers nutrients, food choices, dietary needs, and eating patterns. Individual needs vary with age, health, culture, and personal circumstances. Use this topic page to explore the source material and discuss individual medical nutrition concerns with a qualified professional.

title: Healthy eating basics
text: MyPlate is a visual guide for building balanced meals from food groups. It offers flexible healthy-eating ideas; a single plate pattern is not a personalized treatment plan and may not fit every person's medical or cultural needs. Explore the USDA guide for practical examples.

title: Sleep
text: Sleep supports health and daily functioning. MedlinePlus describes sleep disorders, common symptoms, tests, and treatments. Persistent sleep problems or symptoms affecting daily life deserve an individualized conversation with a qualified healthcare professional.

title: Water in diet
text: Water is needed for normal body functions. Fluid needs can vary with health, activity, weather, pregnancy, and medicines. Some health conditions require individual fluid guidance; ask a qualified professional for advice specific to your situation.

title: Food safety
text: Food safety practices help reduce foodborne illness. CDC guidance covers keeping food clean, separating raw foods, cooking safely, and refrigerating food promptly. Follow the detailed current guidance from CDC for specific handling and storage questions.

title: Exercise and physical fitness
text: Physical activity can support general health. Appropriate activity varies by a person's health, ability, and circumstances. Review MedlinePlus information and ask a healthcare professional about activity that is suitable for an individual medical condition.

title: Talking with your doctor
text: Before a visit, write down your concerns, when symptoms began, and what changes them. Bring a list of medicines, supplements and allergies. Ask questions and take notes about the next steps. This preparation does not determine urgency or diagnose symptoms.

title: Understanding lab results
text: Lab results are one part of a health assessment. Laboratories may use different units and reference ranges. A result outside the range does not by itself establish disease; a result within it does not guarantee health. A clinician interprets results alongside symptoms and history.

title: Medicines
text: Medicines can help treat illness but can also cause side effects and interactions with other medicines, foods or alcohol. Discuss your medicine list and questions with a clinician or pharmacist. This summary does not choose a medicine, check a specific interaction, or advise starting, stopping or changing a dose.

title: Mental health
text: Mental health includes emotional, psychological and social wellbeing. It affects coping, relationships and everyday functioning, and can change with life circumstances. Persistent concerns or difficulties with daily life deserve professional support. This introduction is not a mental health assessment or therapy.

title: Diabetes
text: Diabetes involves blood glucose that is too high and problems with insulin production or use. There are different types. Diagnosis uses clinical assessment and blood tests; care is individualized. This introduction does not diagnose diabetes or interpret your glucose readings.

title: High blood pressure
text: Blood pressure describes blood pushing against artery walls and is recorded as systolic and diastolic values. High blood pressure often has no symptoms. A clinician evaluates measurements and your circumstances. This introduction does not classify your readings or recommend treatment.

title: Vaccines
text: Vaccines train the immune system to recognize and defend against particular germs. Vaccination can help protect people and communities. This introduction explains the general concept; ask a qualified professional for current recommendations suitable for your age, location and health circumstances.

title: Pain
text: Pain is an unpleasant nervous-system signal and can vary in location, intensity and duration. Describe where it is, when it began, what changes it and how it affects daily life to your clinician. This general introduction cannot identify its cause or determine whether waiting is safe.
